subject: chemistry
title: Electrophilic Eclipse: Alkenes and Aromatics
welcome_lead: Track curly arrows in alkene addition and aromatic substitution.
meta_desc: A-Level chemistry adventure on electrophilic addition and substitution.
final_note: You energised the electrophile and conserved every electron.

concepts.def: H on C with more H; +ve on more substituted C.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Pi electrons of C=C attack H of polar H-Br. Curly arrow from C=C to H, second arrow from H-Br bond to Br.

Carbocation intermediate; Br- then attacks. Markovnikov gives more stable (more substituted) cation. Secondary > primary stability.

Br2 polarised by approaching pi electrons. Pi attacks Br+; Br- adds to opposite face (anti addition).

Test for unsaturation: orange Br2(aq) decolourised by alkenes.

Conc HNO3 + conc H2SO4 generates NO2+. Pi electrons attack NO2+, forming Wheland intermediate (sp3 C).

HSO4- removes H+ to restore aromaticity. Product is nitrobenzene. Temperature kept ~50 deg C to avoid dinitration.

mcqs.q: Test for C=C with bromine water?
Why does benzene undergo electrophilic SUBSTITUTION but alkenes undergo electrophilic ADDITION?
options: The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
Benzene reacts the same way as alkenes — by addition across one of its double bonds.
Substitution preserves benzene's stable delocalised pi system; addition would destroy aromaticity at a large energetic cost.
Benzene cannot react with electrophiles at all.

mcqs.q: How do alkenes typically react with bromine?
options: The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
A curly arrow shows the direction in which heat is flowing in the reaction.
Bromine substitutes for a hydrogen on the alkene, releasing HBr.
By electrophilic addition — bromine adds across the double bond to form a dibromoalkane.

mcqs.q: What does a curly arrow in an organic mechanism represent?
options: A curly arrow shows the direction in which heat is flowing in the reaction.
The alkene polymerises with bromine to form a long chain.
The movement of a pair of electrons from where they are to where they end up.
A curly arrow shows the movement of an atom from one position to another.
